title: Arabia Before Islam and the Meccan Period
bigQuestion: What was Mecca like around the year 600, and how does that world help us read the earliest surahs?

story.title: A Merchant's Word
story.kicker: In a caravan city where a promise was a kind of money, one merchant's promise turned into a new kind of message.
paragraphs: Picture Mecca around the year 600. It sits in a dry valley in western Arabia, ringed by bare hills. There is no river and almost no farmland. What Mecca has is a well called Zamzam, a square stone building called the Kaaba, and a road. Caravans of camels pass through on their way between Yemen in the south and Syria in the north. They carry leather, spices, cloth and incense. The people of Mecca make their living by trading, guarding and feeding these caravans.

In a city like this, a merchant's word is his bond. There are no courts and no police. A tribe protects its own members, and a person without a tribe has no protection at all. So trust matters. A merchant who cheats on weights or breaks a promise loses more than one sale. He loses his name. Muslim tradition says that one young merchant of the tribe of Quraysh was known for keeping his word so well that people called him al-Amin, "the trustworthy." His name was Muhammad.

The sira, the traditional life story of Muhammad, tells that he led trading trips for a wealthy widow named Khadijah. She was impressed by his honesty, and they married. For years he lived the life of a respected Meccan trader. But the sira also says he liked to go alone to a cave on a hill outside the city called Hira, to think. He was about forty years old when, Muslims believe, something happened there that changed everything.

According to Muslim tradition, an angel came to him in the cave and said one word: "Read." The words that followed became the first lines of the Qur'an. Muhammad came home shaking and told Khadijah what had happened. She believed him first. The merchant known for his word now had a message he said came from God. Over the next twelve years in Mecca, that message would win him a small band of followers, a large number of enemies, and finally the loss of his home city.

This chapter looks at the world Muhammad was born into, the story of his life in Mecca as Muslims tell it, and the surahs that tradition says come from those years. We will also ask a historian's question: which parts of this story can be checked against outside evidence, and which parts rest on Muslim tradition alone?
story.think: Why would a reputation for honesty matter so much in a city with no courts? What does that tell you about how people in Mecca would first have judged a new message?

lessons.title: A Land of Tribes and Trade
lessons.mainIdea: Arabia around 600 was a land of tribes and trade routes, where a person's safety came from the tribe and a city's wealth came from the caravans.
reading: Arabia is a huge peninsula, mostly desert. Around the year 600, most of its people belonged to a *tribe*: a large family group that shared an ancestor, a name and a duty to protect one another. Some tribes were *Bedouin*, herders who moved with their camels and sheep to find grass. Others settled in towns built around wells and oases. There was no king of Arabia and no single law. If a member of your tribe was hurt, your tribe took revenge or demanded payment. That was the only justice most people had.

Trade tied the peninsula together. Camel *caravan*s carried goods from Yemen in the south, where incense grew, up to Syria and the Mediterranean world. Along the way they stopped at towns like Mecca, Yathrib (later called Medina) and Ta'if. Mecca had a special advantage. It lay near the route, it had a well, and it held a shrine that drew visitors. Meccans grew wealthy by hosting pilgrims, guarding caravans and trading at seasonal fairs.

Poetry was the great art of Arabia. Tribes held contests, and a poet who could praise his own tribe and mock its rivals was a kind of celebrity. People memorized long poems and passed them down by voice. This matters for the study of the Qur'an. The Qur'an came into a culture that prized spoken Arabic, rhyme and memory. Muslims and scholars alike note that the Qur'an's early listeners judged it first by how it sounded.

Tradition also describes a harsh side of this world. Warfare between tribes was common. Wealth was unequal, and a widow, an orphan or a person without a tribe could be cheated with little chance of help. Historians say these were the problems of Mecca and the surrounding tribes in the years just before Islam. As we will see, the earliest surahs speak to them directly.

words.d: a large family group sharing an ancestor and a duty to protect its members; the main unit of Arabian society around 600
Arab herders who moved from place to place with their animals
a group of traders traveling together, usually with camels, for safety

look.title: Distances on the Trade Road
look.cite: Approximate straight-line distances between the cities; caravan routes were longer
look.prompt: A caravan traveled about 20 miles a day. Roughly how many days would it take to go from Mecca to Damascus? Why would such a trip need protection?

check.q: Around the year 600, where did most people in Arabia get protection and justice?
choices: From the priests of the Kaaba
check.why: There was no king or shared law; a person's tribe protected its members and took revenge or payment for harm.

check.q: Why did Mecca become wealthy?
choices: It hosted pilgrims and caravans on a trade route
It was the capital of Persia
check.why: Mecca had little farmland; its wealth came from the well, the shrine and the caravan trade passing through.

check.q: Which art was most prized in Arabia before Islam, according to tradition and historians?
check.why: Poetry contests and memorized poems were central; this shaped how the Qur'an's first listeners heard it.

lessons.title: Two Empires and Many Faiths
lessons.mainIdea: Arabia lay between the Byzantine and Persian empires, and Jews, Christians and followers of the old Arabian gods all lived there.
reading: North of Arabia stood two great empires. To the northwest was the *Byzantine* Empire, the Greek-speaking Roman empire ruled from Constantinople, whose official faith was Christianity. To the northeast was the Persian Empire of the Sasanian kings, whose main religion was Zoroastrianism. From 602 to 628 these two empires fought a long, exhausting war. Some Arab tribes on the borders fought for one side or the other. The Qur'an's Surah 30, Ar-Rum ("The Romans"), opens by mentioning a Roman defeat, and most commentators tie this to that war.

Arabia was not only a land of the old gods. Jewish communities had lived in Yathrib and other oasis towns for centuries. They farmed date palms, worked as craftsmen and kept their own scriptures and customs. Christian communities lived in the north near the Byzantine border, in the south in Najran, and across the Red Sea in Abyssinia (today's Ethiopia), a Christian kingdom. Christian monks and traders passed along the caravan roads. Stories of Ibrahim (Abraham), Musa (Moses) and Isa (Jesus) were known in Arabia before the Qur'an.

Most Arabs, though, followed the traditional religion of their tribes. They honored many gods and spirits, kept sacred stones and trees, and made pilgrimages to shrines. Some Arabs, tradition says, were *hanif*s: people who rejected the many gods and sought the one God of Ibrahim without joining Judaism or Christianity. Historians debate how many hanifs there really were. The word appears in the Qur'an, which calls Ibrahim a hanif (3:67).

This mixed world matters for reading the Qur'an. Its audience already knew the names of the biblical prophets, the idea of one God, and the practices of the old Arabian religion. The Qur'an speaks to all three groups. It calls Jews and Christians "People of the Book," it argues with the followers of the tribal gods, and it presents itself as confirming the message of earlier prophets.

words.d: the Greek-speaking eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople and officially Christian
the Persian ruling dynasty (c. 224–651) whose main religion was Zoroastrianism
in the Qur'an and Muslim tradition, a person who worshipped the one God of Ibrahim without being a Jew or Christian

look.title: Who Was Listening?
look.text: Imagine three people hearing a new message in Mecca around 613: a Jewish date farmer visiting from Yathrib, a Christian trader from Abyssinia, and a Meccan who keeps a small stone idol at home. The message says: there is one God, Ibrahim served him, and a day of judgment is coming.
look.prompt: Which parts of that message would each listener already recognize, and which parts would be new or hard for each of them to accept?

check.q: Which two empires bordered Arabia around 600?
check.why: The Byzantine (eastern Roman) and Sasanian Persian empires lay north of Arabia and fought a long war from 602 to 628.

check.q: Which Qur'an surah is named for the Romans and opens with a mention of their defeat?
check.why: Ar-Rum means 'the Romans'; commentators link its opening to the Byzantine–Persian war.

check.q: In Muslim tradition, what is a hanif?
choices: A person seeking the one God of Ibrahim without being a Jew or Christian
check.why: The Qur'an uses hanif for Ibrahim (3:67); tradition applies it to Arabs who rejected the many gods before Islam.

lessons.title: The Kaaba and Its Gods
lessons.mainIdea: Before Islam, the Kaaba in Mecca was a shrine to many gods, and the tribe of Quraysh gained wealth and honor by guarding it.
reading: At the center of Mecca stood the *Kaaba*, a cube-shaped stone building. Its name simply means "cube." Muslim tradition says Ibrahim (Abraham) and his son Ismail (Ishmael) built it to worship the one God, and that over the centuries the Arabs filled it with idols. Historians can confirm that the Kaaba was an important shrine before Islam. By around 600, tradition says, it held images and stones for many gods, often counted at 360. Three goddesses, al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat, were especially honored, and the Qur'an names them (53:19–20).

The tribe of *Quraysh* controlled Mecca and the Kaaba. Different clans of Quraysh held different duties: keeping the keys, giving water to pilgrims, feeding them. Each year, Arabs from many tribes came on pilgrimage. During certain sacred months, fighting was forbidden, so trade fairs could be held safely. The shrine, the truce and the market fed one another. This is why, tradition says, the leaders of Quraysh reacted so strongly to a message that attacked the gods of the Kaaba.

Pilgrims walked around the Kaaba, a practice called *tawaf*. They also touched a dark stone set into its corner, called the Black Stone. Muslims kept both practices after Islam, but they gave them a new meaning: circling the house that, they believe, Ibrahim built for the one God. Today the Kaaba stands inside the Great Mosque of Mecca and is the direction Muslims face in prayer.

Quraysh's own name appears in the Qur'an. Surah 106, called Quraysh, is only four verses long. In Pickthall's translation it speaks of the tribe's winter and summer caravans and tells them to worship "the Lord of this House," who fed them and kept them safe. Commentators read it as tying Mecca's trade and safety to the one God rather than to the many idols.

words.d: the cube-shaped shrine in Mecca; Muslims believe Ibrahim and Ismail built it, and they face it in prayer
the Meccan tribe that guarded the Kaaba and controlled the city's trade; Muhammad's tribe
walking around the Kaaba, a practice older than Islam that Muslims continued with new meaning

look.title: Surah Quraysh, Paraphrased
look.text: The surah speaks of the bonds of Quraysh, their journeys in winter and summer, and then tells them to serve the Lord of this House, the one who fed them when they were hungry and made them safe from fear.
look.cite: Qur'an 106:1–4 (Surah Quraysh), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What two things does this surah say the Lord of the House gave Quraysh? How does that connect to what you learned about Mecca's trade and truce?

check.q: Which tribe controlled Mecca and the Kaaba around 600?
check.why: Quraysh guarded the Kaaba, hosted pilgrims and ran Mecca's trade; Muhammad belonged to this tribe.

check.q: What does the word Kaaba mean?
check.why: Kaaba means 'cube,' describing the shrine's shape.

check.q: Why, according to tradition, did the leaders of Quraysh oppose a message against the gods of the Kaaba?
choices: The shrine, sacred truce and markets brought them wealth and honor
They preferred to worship in Yathrib
check.why: Tradition ties Quraysh's opposition to the way the shrine, pilgrimage and trade fairs supported the city.

lessons.title: Where the Story Comes From
lessons.mainIdea: The story of Muhammad's life comes from the sira, written down more than a century after his death, and from the Qur'an itself.
reading: Where does the story of Muhammad's life come from? Not from the Qur'an alone. The Qur'an rarely tells events in order and names Muhammad only four times. The main source is the *sira*, the traditional biography. The most important early sira was written by Ibn Ishaq, who died c. 767, about 135 years after Muhammad's death. His work survives mainly in a later edited version by Ibn Hisham (died c. 833). Other early sources include al-Waqidi's book on the Prophet's campaigns and the *hadith* collections, reports of the Prophet's words and actions.

The sira writers gathered oral reports that had passed from person to person for generations. They tried to give a chain of names showing who told whom. Muslim scholars developed careful methods to judge these chains. Even so, the sira contains different versions of the same event, and its authors sometimes say so themselves. Al-Tabari, a great historian and commentator (died 923), often records two or three versions side by side.

Historians outside the tradition ask a different question: what can be checked? A few things can. Sources written by non-Muslims in the 630s and 640s mention an Arab prophet and Arab armies. Early Qur'an manuscripts, including pages held in Birmingham, England, have been dated by radiocarbon to around the mid-600s. Coins and inscriptions from the 600s name Muhammad. These confirm the broad outline. They do not confirm the details of individual stories, which many historians treat as tradition rather than proven fact.

In this course we tell the life of Muhammad as Muslim tradition tells it, because that is the story that shaped how Muslims read the Qur'an. We mark dates with "c." (around) and say "tradition says" or "the sira reports." Both approaches, the believer's and the historian's, take the story seriously. They simply ask different questions of it.

words.d: the traditional biography of Muhammad; the earliest major one is by Ibn Ishaq (died c. 767), preserved by Ibn Hisham
a report of something Muhammad said, did or approved, passed down with a chain of names
stories and reports passed by word of mouth before being written down

look.title: How Far the Sources Sit from the Events
look.cite: Standard dates for the authors' deaths, as given in reference works; the works were completed in their lifetimes
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Muhammad's death and Ibn Ishaq's sira? Why might historians and believers weigh that gap differently?

check.q: What is the sira?
check.why: The sira is the traditional life story of Muhammad; Ibn Ishaq's is the earliest major one.

check.q: In whose later edition does Ibn Ishaq's sira mainly survive?
check.why: Ibn Hisham (died c. 833) edited and preserved Ibn Ishaq's work.

check.q: Which kind of evidence do historians say confirms the broad outline, but not the details, of Muhammad's life?
choices: Early coins, inscriptions, manuscripts and non-Muslim writings from the 600s
check.why: Outside sources from the 600s name an Arab prophet and early Qur'an pages, but they do not verify each story.

lessons.title: A Merchant of Quraysh
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition says Muhammad was born in Mecca c. 570, orphaned young, raised by his grandfather and uncle, and became a trusted merchant married to Khadijah.
reading: According to Muslim tradition, Muhammad was born in Mecca around the year 570 into the clan of Hashim, part of the tribe of Quraysh. His father, Abdullah, died before he was born. His mother, Amina, died when he was about six. His grandfather Abd al-Muttalib took him in, and when the grandfather died, his uncle *Abu Talib* raised him. Abu Talib was not wealthy, but he was respected, and he protected Muhammad for the rest of his life. The Qur'an seems to look back on this childhood when it says God found the Prophet an orphan and gave him shelter (93:6).

As a young man, tradition says, Muhammad worked in trade. He traveled with caravans to Syria, and one story tells of a Christian monk named Bahira who recognized something special in the boy. Historians treat this as a pious story rather than proven fact. What the sources agree on is his reputation. He was called al-Amin, the trustworthy, and Meccans asked him to settle disputes. One well-known story says that when Quraysh rebuilt the Kaaba, the clans argued over who should set the Black Stone in place. Muhammad had them lift it together on a cloth.

Around 595, tradition says, he married *Khadijah*, a wealthy widow and merchant who had hired him to lead her caravans. She was about fifteen years older than he was. They had several children, including daughters; Fatima is the best known. For about twenty-five years, until her death, Khadijah was his only wife. Muslims remember her as the first person to believe in his message, and Shia and Sunni Muslims alike honor her.

Tradition presents these years quietly. Muhammad was a family man and a trader, not a poet or a priest. The Qur'an itself says he was not known for reciting books before the revelation (29:48). Muslims read this as a sign that the Qur'an came from God, not from Muhammad's learning. Historians note that we know almost nothing about these years from outside sources. Both agree on this: whatever happened next happened to an ordinary, respected man of Mecca.

words.d: Muhammad's uncle, who raised him and protected him in Mecca until his death c. 619
Muhammad's first wife, a wealthy merchant; Muslims remember her as the first to believe his message
'the trustworthy,' the nickname tradition says Meccans gave Muhammad

look.title: The Black Stone and the Cloth
look.text: The sira reports that when Quraysh rebuilt the Kaaba, each clan wanted the honor of placing the Black Stone. They agreed to let the next man through the gate decide. It was Muhammad. He spread a cloth, put the stone on it, had a leader from each clan hold an edge, and then set the stone himself.
look.prompt: What problem did this solution solve, and what does the story want the listener to think about Muhammad's character? Why might a historian call this a 'pious story'?

check.q: According to tradition, who raised Muhammad after his grandfather died?
check.why: Abu Talib, his uncle, raised and protected him; his mother had died when he was about six.

check.q: What was Khadijah's role before her marriage to Muhammad?
choices: A wealthy merchant who hired him to lead caravans
check.why: Tradition says Khadijah was a wealthy widow and trader who employed Muhammad before marrying him c. 595.

check.q: How do historians treat the story of the monk Bahira?
choices: As a verse of the Qur'an
As a pious story from tradition, not proven fact
check.why: The Bahira story comes only from later Muslim tradition and cannot be checked against outside sources.

lessons.title: The Cave and the First Words
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe the Qur'an's first revelation came to Muhammad c. 610 in a cave on Mount Hira, beginning with the word "Read."
reading: Muslim tradition says Muhammad often went alone to a cave on a hill outside Mecca called *Hira*. There, around the year 610, during the month of Ramadan, an angel appeared to him. The angel, later named as Jibril (Gabriel), commanded, "Read" (or "Recite"; the Arabic iqra can mean both). Muhammad answered that he could not read. Tradition says the angel pressed him hard, three times, and then spoke the words that Muslims believe are the first *revelation*: the opening five verses of Surah 96, Al-Alaq ("The Clot").

Those five verses say that God created humans from a clot, that God is generous, and that God taught by the pen what humans did not know. Tradition tells that Muhammad hurried home trembling and asked Khadijah to cover him with a cloak. She comforted him. Then she took him to her cousin Waraqa, an old man who knew the Christian and Jewish scriptures. Waraqa, the sira says, told them this was the same kind of message that came to Musa (Moses).

Muslims call this night *Laylat al-Qadr*, the Night of Power, and the Qur'an speaks of it in Surah 97. Many Muslims mark it in the last ten nights of Ramadan. After the first revelation, tradition says, there was a pause of months in which nothing came, and Muhammad feared he had been abandoned. Then, Muslims believe, Surah 93, Ad-Duha ("The Morning Hours"), came to reassure him: his Lord had not forsaken him.

For Muslims, this is the beginning of the Qur'an. For historians, it is an event known only through later tradition and through the text itself. Notice one thing both can see: the first word is a command to read or recite, and the first surah speaks of the pen. From its first lines, the Qur'an presents itself as a message meant to be spoken, learned and passed on.

words.d: the hill and cave outside Mecca where, Muslims believe, the first revelation came c. 610
a message that Muslims believe God sent to Muhammad through the angel Jibril; the Qur'an is the collection of these messages
'the Night of Power,' the night in Ramadan when Muslims believe the Qur'an first came down (Surah 97)

look.title: The First Five Verses
look.text: Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot. Read: And thy Lord is the Most Bounteous, Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not.
look.cite: Qur'an 96:1–5 (Surah Al-Alaq), Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Which word is repeated, and what three things does the passage say about God? Why might a message that begins this way have been heard as a message about learning?

check.q: Where do Muslims believe the first revelation came to Muhammad?
choices: In a cave on Mount Hira
check.why: Tradition places the first revelation in the cave of Hira, on a hill outside Mecca, c. 610.

check.q: Which surah do Muslims hold contains the first words revealed?
check.why: Most Muslim scholars hold that 96:1–5, beginning 'Read,' were the first verses revealed.

check.q: What does the Arabic word iqra mean?
check.why: Iqra can mean both 'read' and 'recite'; Pickthall translates it as 'Read.'

lessons.title: The Message and the Opposition
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition says Muhammad preached one God, judgment and care for the weak; a few Meccans believed, but the leaders of Quraysh turned against him.
reading: For about three years, tradition says, Muhammad shared the message only privately. Khadijah believed first. Then came his young cousin Ali, his friend the merchant Abu Bakr, and his adopted son Zayd. Around 613, Muslims believe, the Qur'an told him to warn his own clan and then the city (26:214, 15:94). He began to preach in public. The message was simple and sharp. There is one God. The idols are nothing. A day of judgment is coming. The rich must not cheat the poor, the orphan or the widow.

The first Muslims were a mixed group. Some were young men from good families. Others were poor, foreign or enslaved. *Bilal*, an enslaved man of African descent, became a Muslim and was, tradition says, tortured by his owner until Abu Bakr bought and freed him. Later Bilal became the first *muezzin*, the one who calls Muslims to prayer. Muslims remember him as proof that the message reached across rank and race.

The leaders of Quraysh, tradition says, first laughed. Then they grew angry. They asked Abu Talib to silence his nephew, and he refused. They offered Muhammad money and power to stop; the sira says he refused too. Some Muslims were beaten, and Meccans mocked the Prophet as a poet, a soothsayer or a madman. Several Meccan surahs answer these charges directly, which is one reason commentators date them to these years (for example, 52:29–30 and 69:41–42).

Historians note that opposition made sense from Quraysh's side. Their wealth and honor rested on the Kaaba, the pilgrimage and the peace of the sacred months. A message that called the Kaaba's gods false and that criticized the rich threatened the whole system. Muslim tradition says the same thing but from the other side: the leaders rejected the truth to protect their power. Both readings agree on what was at stake.

words.d: an enslaved Abyssinian man who became an early Muslim, was freed, and became the first caller to prayer
the person who calls Muslims to the five daily prayers
a Meccan merchant and close friend of Muhammad; one of the first Muslims and later the first caliph

look.title: The Orphan and the Beggar
look.text: Near the end of Surah 93, the Qur'an tells its listener not to treat the orphan harshly and not to turn the beggar away, and to speak of the Lord's favor.
look.cite: Qur'an 93:9–11 (Surah Ad-Duha), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The surah earlier reminds the Prophet that he was once an orphan himself. How does that change the way you read these commands?

check.q: According to tradition, who was the first person to believe Muhammad's message?
check.why: Muslims remember Khadijah, his wife, as the first believer, followed by Ali, Abu Bakr and Zayd.

check.q: Who is Bilal in Muslim tradition?
choices: A freed enslaved man who became the first muezzin
check.why: Bilal, freed by Abu Bakr, became the first caller to prayer and is honored across the Muslim world.

check.q: Why does tradition say the leaders of Quraysh opposed the message?
choices: They wanted to move the Kaaba to Yathrib
They were followers of the Persian religion
It threatened the gods, pilgrimage and trade that gave them wealth and honor
check.why: Both tradition and historians tie the opposition to the Kaaba's role in Mecca's economy and honor.

lessons.title: Boycott, Abyssinia and the Year of Sorrow
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition tells of a boycott, a group of Muslims sheltered by a Christian king in Abyssinia, and the deaths of Khadijah and Abu Talib in c. 619.
reading: Around 615, tradition says, the pressure on the Muslims grew so heavy that Muhammad sent a group of them across the Red Sea to *Abyssinia*, a Christian kingdom (today's Ethiopia). Its king, whom the Arabs called the Negus, received them. Quraysh sent envoys to demand their return. The sira tells that the Muslim spokesman, Jafar, recited part of Surah 19, Maryam, which tells of Maryam (Mary) and the birth of Isa (Jesus). The king, the story says, wept and refused to hand them over. Muslims often tell this as a story of a Christian ruler protecting Muslims.

In Mecca, tradition says, Quraysh declared a *boycott* of Muhammad's whole clan around 616. No one would trade with the clan of Hashim or marry into it. The clan, Muslims and non-Muslims together, was shut into a valley on the edge of the city for about three years. Food was scarce. The boycott ended around 619 when some Meccans, ashamed, tore up the agreement. Historians note that the details vary among the sources, but the boycott appears in all the main accounts.

Soon after, tradition says, Muhammad lost the two people who had protected him most. Khadijah died, and then Abu Talib. Muslims call c. 619 the *Year of Sorrow*. Abu Talib had never become a Muslim, but as head of the clan he had shielded his nephew. His successor as clan head, Abu Lahab, withdrew that protection. Surah 111 is read by commentators as a condemnation of Abu Lahab by name.

With no protector in Mecca, Muhammad tried the nearby town of Ta'if, tradition says, and was driven out with stones. Yet the sira also tells of hope from an unexpected place. Pilgrims from Yathrib, a town far to the north, heard him and were moved. They would return. This is where the next chapter begins.

words.d: the Christian kingdom across the Red Sea (today's Ethiopia) where, tradition says, early Muslims found shelter c. 615
refusing to trade or deal with a group in order to pressure it; Quraysh used one against Muhammad's clan c. 616–619
the Muslim name for c. 619, when Khadijah and Abu Talib both died

look.title: A Recitation Before a King
look.text: In the sira's account, the Negus asks the Muslim refugees what their prophet says about Isa (Jesus). Jafar recites from Surah 19, Maryam. The story says the king drew a line on the ground with his staff and said the difference between his faith and theirs was no wider than that line.
look.prompt: Why might the Muslims have chosen Surah 19 to recite to a Christian king? What does the story about the line say about how early Muslims wanted their relationship with Christians to be remembered?

check.q: Where did some early Muslims find shelter around 615, according to tradition?
check.why: Tradition says a Christian king in Abyssinia (Ethiopia) protected the Muslim refugees.

check.q: Which surah does the sira say Jafar recited to the Negus?
check.why: Surah 19, named for Maryam (Mary), tells of the birth of Isa, which spoke to a Christian audience.

check.q: Why is c. 619 called the Year of Sorrow?
choices: Khadijah and Abu Talib both died that year
check.why: Muhammad lost both his wife and his protecting uncle in about 619, leaving him exposed in Mecca.

lessons.title: One God and Nothing Beside Him
lessons.mainIdea: The Meccan surahs' central theme is tawhid, the oneness of God, stated most tightly in Surah 112.
reading: Muslim scholars divide the Qur'an's 114 surahs into Meccan and Medinan, according to whether they were revealed before or after the move to Medina in 622. About 86 are counted as Meccan, though scholars differ on a few. Meccan surahs tend to be short, with strong rhythm and rhyme. They speak to a city that did not yet accept the message. Their first theme is *tawhid*, the oneness of God.

Surah 112, Al-Ikhlas ("Sincerity" or "Purity"), is the tightest statement of this theme. It is four short verses. It says God is one, that all depend on him, that he was not born and did not give birth, and that nothing is like him. Muslims often say this surah is worth a third of the Qur'an, a saying reported in hadith. Many Muslims recite it daily. Commentators read the line about not begetting as an answer both to Meccans who called angels God's daughters and to Christian teaching about Jesus as God's son.

The Meccan surahs argue for one God from the world itself. They point to rain, crops, the night sky, the camel, the birth of a child, and ask who made these. The Qur'an calls these *ayat*, signs, the same word used for its own verses. The argument is not that God exists; the Meccans already believed in a high god they called Allah. The argument is that this God has no partners and alone deserves worship. The Qur'an calls giving God partners *shirk*, and it treats shirk as the gravest error.

Read closely, Surah 112 shows the Meccan style. No story, no law, no names. Just a claim, stated in the fewest words. Sunni, Shia and Sufi readers all treat tawhid as the heart of Islam, though Sufi writers often add a further meaning: that the believer's own self should vanish before God's oneness. The surah supports many readings because it says so little and claims so much.

words.d: the oneness of God; the central belief of Islam and the main theme of the Meccan surahs
a surah that Muslim scholars date to before the hijra of 622; usually short and rhythmic
giving God partners or equals; in the Qur'an, the gravest error
'signs'; the Qur'an uses the word both for its verses and for the evidence of God in nature

look.title: Surah Al-Ikhlas in Full
look.text: Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him.
look.cite: Qur'an 112:1–4 (Surah Al-Ikhlas), Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The surah begins with 'Say.' Who is being told to say this, and to whom? List the four claims it makes in your own words.

check.q: About how many of the Qur'an's 114 surahs are counted as Meccan?
check.why: Traditional counts put about 86 surahs in Mecca and 28 in Medina, though scholars differ on a few.

check.q: What does tawhid mean?
check.why: Tawhid is the belief that God is one and has no partners; Surah 112 states it most tightly.

check.q: In the Qur'an, what is shirk?
check.why: Shirk is the opposite of tawhid; the Meccan surahs argue against it constantly.

lessons.title: Judgment and Justice for the Weak
lessons.mainIdea: Meccan surahs warn of a Day of Judgment and tie true religion to how a person treats the orphan, the beggar and the poor.
reading: The second great theme of the Meccan surahs is the *Day of Judgment*. Many short surahs describe it in vivid pictures: the sky split, the mountains scattered like wool, the sun folded up, every person shown what they did (81:1–14 is one example). The Qur'an says each person will be judged alone, and that deeds will be weighed. Meccans, tradition says, found this hard to accept. Several surahs record their objection: how can bones and dust live again? The Qur'an answers that the God who made a person once can make them again.

Judgment in the Qur'an is not only about belief. Again and again, the Meccan surahs tie it to justice. Surah 107, Al-Ma'un ("Small Kindnesses"), asks who denies religion, and answers: the one who pushes away the orphan and does not urge feeding the poor. Surah 104 condemns the one who piles up wealth and counts it. Surah 83 opens by condemning those who cheat on weights and measures. Commentators read these against Mecca's trading economy, where such cheating was a real problem.

This is why many readers, Muslim and not, describe the earliest message as social as well as religious. The Qur'an's own word for a right act is often *salih*, "good" or "sound." Faith and good works appear together dozens of times: "those who believe and do good works." Surah 90 speaks of "the steep path": freeing a slave and feeding the hungry on a day of hunger. Historians note that this teaching appealed to the poor and the young in Mecca, and worried the wealthy.

Muslim readers connect this theme to *zakat*, the required giving to the poor that later became one of the Five Pillars. The word appears in Meccan surahs before the rules for it were set in Medina. Sufi readers stress the inner side: greed as a disease of the heart. Modern Muslim writers often stress the social side: the Qur'an as a call for fairness. All of them are reading the same short surahs.

words.d: the day when, the Qur'an says, every person will be raised and judged for their deeds
'good' or 'sound'; the Qur'an pairs faith with doing good works
giving a share of one's wealth to the poor; a duty named in Meccan surahs and set out in rules in Medina

look.title: Who Denies Religion?
look.text: Surah 107 opens with a question: have you seen the one who denies religion? It answers that this is the person who pushes the orphan away and does not urge others to feed the poor. It then warns those who pray but are careless in prayer, who only want to be seen, and who refuse small kindnesses.
look.cite: Qur'an 107:1–7 (Surah Al-Ma'un), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: According to this surah, how can you tell whether someone truly holds their religion? What does that say about what 'religion' means here?

check.q: In Surah 107, who is the person who 'denies religion'?
choices: The one who travels with caravans
The one who pushes away the orphan and does not feed the poor
The one who prays at night
check.why: Al-Ma'un ties denying religion to mistreating the orphan and neglecting the poor.

check.q: Which objection to the message do Meccan surahs record and answer?
choices: That there is no God at all
That the Kaaba should be destroyed
That Arabic is not a holy language
That bones and dust cannot live again
check.why: Several surahs quote the Meccans' doubt about resurrection and answer that God can create again.

check.q: What phrase does the Qur'an repeat dozens of times to tie faith to action?
choices: Those who believe and do good works
check.why: 'Those who believe and do good works' is a recurring pair; salih means 'good' or 'sound.'

lessons.title: The Night Journey
lessons.mainIdea: Muslim tradition tells of a night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and up through the heavens, tied to Qur'an 17:1 and remembered every year.
reading: Around 620, tradition says, in the hardest years in Mecca, Muhammad had an experience that Muslims call the *Isra* and *Mi'raj*, the Night Journey and the Ascent. The Qur'an mentions it in one verse. Surah 17, Al-Isra, opens by praising God who carried his servant by night from "the Inviolable Place of Worship" to "the Far Distant Place of Worship" (Pickthall's wording). Muslims read the first as the Kaaba in Mecca and the second as Jerusalem. The verse says God showed him some of his signs.

The sira and hadith fill in the rest. Tradition says the angel Jibril brought a winged animal called Buraq. Muhammad rode to Jerusalem, where he led the earlier prophets in prayer. Then he rose through the seven heavens, meeting Adam, Isa (Jesus), Musa (Moses), Ibrahim (Abraham) and others. At the highest point, tradition says, God gave the command of fifty daily prayers, and on Musa's advice Muhammad asked for it to be lightened until it became five. This is how Muslims explain the five daily prayers.

Muslims have read this story in different ways. Many hold it was a bodily journey. Some early reports, including one attributed to the Prophet's wife Aisha, say his body did not leave Mecca and the journey was of the spirit. Sufi writers treat the ascent as a picture of the soul's journey toward God. All of these readings are found within Islam, and most Muslims mark the night each year on the 27th of the month of Rajab.

The story shaped places. The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, built c. 691, stands where Muslims believe the ascent began, and Jerusalem became the third holiest city for Muslims after Mecca and Medina. The story also ties Islam to the earlier prophets: in it, Muhammad prays with Musa and Isa, not against them. Historians can say when the buildings went up and when the story was written down; they cannot check the journey itself, and they do not try to.

words.d: the Night Journey, which Muslims believe took Muhammad from Mecca to Jerusalem (Qur'an 17:1)
the Ascent through the heavens that tradition says followed the Night Journey
the winged animal that, in tradition, carried Muhammad on the Night Journey

look.title: One Verse, a Whole Tradition
look.text: The verse praises God, who carried his servant by night from the sacred place of worship to the far-off place of worship, whose surroundings God has blessed, in order to show him some of God's signs; God is the one who hears and sees.
look.cite: Qur'an 17:1 (Surah Al-Isra), paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The verse does not name Jerusalem, Buraq or the seven heavens. Where does each of those details come from, and why does it matter to know that?

check.q: Which Qur'an verse do Muslims connect to the Night Journey?
check.why: Surah 17, Al-Isra, opens with the verse about God carrying his servant by night.

check.q: In tradition, what did Muhammad receive at the highest point of the Mi'raj?
choices: The command of daily prayers, reduced to five
check.why: Tradition says fifty prayers were reduced to five, which is how Muslims explain the five daily prayers.

check.q: Which building in Jerusalem stands where Muslims believe the ascent began?
check.why: The Dome of the Rock (c. 691) marks the site; Jerusalem is Islam's third holiest city.

lessons.title: What Historians Can and Cannot Confirm
lessons.mainIdea: Outside evidence confirms that Muhammad lived, that Arabs conquered widely soon after, and that the Qur'an is early; the details of the Meccan story rest on tradition.
reading: Historians work from evidence that can be dated and checked. For the Meccan period, that evidence is thin. No document written in Mecca in the 610s survives. The earliest sira was written more than a century later. So historians ask what can be confirmed by *outside sources*, writings by people who were not Muslims, and by *material evidence*, such as coins, inscriptions and manuscripts.

Several things can be confirmed. A Greek text from the 630s mentions a prophet who had appeared among the Arabs. An Armenian history from the 660s describes Muhammad as a merchant who taught the Arabs about the God of Abraham. Arab armies conquered Syria, Egypt and Persia in the 630s and 640s; that is documented by many sources. Coins and inscriptions naming Muhammad appear by the late 600s. Qur'an manuscripts, including the Birmingham folios, have been radiocarbon dated to the mid-600s, showing the text existed early.

Other things cannot be confirmed from outside. The cave of Hira, the boycott, the refugees in Abyssinia, the Night Journey: these are known only from Muslim tradition and from hints in the Qur'an. This does not mean they did not happen. It means historians cannot test them the way they test a dated coin. Some historians, such as Fred Donner, argue that the Qur'an's own text fits the world of early seventh-century Arabia well. Others are more skeptical about the sira's details. The debate is ongoing.

Muslim scholars have their own long tradition of weighing sources, judging hadith by their chains of names and the honesty of each reporter. The two methods overlap but are not the same. In a public school, we can hold both in view. We can say what Muslims believe and why, and we can say what historians can show. Keeping the two clear is a skill, and it is the skill this course practices.

words.d: writings by people who were not part of a tradition, used by historians to check that tradition's accounts
physical objects such as coins, inscriptions and manuscripts that can be dated and examined
a scientific method for estimating the age of organic material, such as the parchment of a manuscript
